transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-03-07
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Evan Marshall (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Marta González (Vesper CTO), Liam O'Neill (ML Eng), Sofia Rojas (Product)
Recording note: audio mostly clear, a couple of overlap / cut words, some auto-caps and punctuation errors.

[00:00] Evan: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. I'll do a really quick intro — I'm Evan, I'm the AE on the Vesper account, and then Priya will lead the Optimize lab.
[00:12] Priya: Hi! super excited. I know Vesper wanted a hands-on look at how batching and prefix/KV caching trade off against cost and latency, and we'll run a couple sims with your traffic profile if you shared that.
[00:25] Marta: Yep, thanks. We did upload a sample trace - it's a mix of short chat queries and a few long generation requests, and peak concurrency around 420 rps.
[00:36] Liam: Quick add — most of our sessions are multi-turn, around 3-6 turns, and we keep user context for about 30 minutes session window. We currently run a homegrown cache but it's pretty brittle.
[00:49] Priya: Great context. So agenda — 1) quick qualification of SLOs and constraints, 2) console walkthrough of Optimize recommendations, 3) run sensitivity sims (batch size, prefix hit rate, session TTL), 4) Q/A and next steps.

[01:10] Marta: Sounds good. Our hard constraints: 200 ms P95 at peak for single-turn queries, and at most 20% of our current inference spend increase to hit that SLO. We really want to avoid wholesale model downsizing because accuracy matters.
[01:25] Evan: Understood. Priya, do you want to jump into the console?

[01:32] Priya: Yep. I'm sharing my screen - Slides and the Optimize console. (link shown: https://console.redwood.ai/optimize/sandbox/vep) Note: the console export sometimes shows "Redwood Optimise" in captions because our ASR pulls UK spelling, heh.
[01:50] Priya: First thing — Optimize ingests a traffic trace and suggests batching, concurrency and KV/prefix cache parameters. For Vesper's profile we see a long tail of short prompts and a small but costy set of long-generations.
[02:05] Liam: The trace we uploaded was truncated to last 48 hours, does that give you representative sequence lengths?
[02:12] Priya: It's enough to build a first-order sim. We'll flag sensitivity to seasonality later. Ok, on screen: Sim 1 baseline (no prefetched prefix, conservative batching): avg batch size 1.6, token cost baseline $X. You'll see the P95 latency is at 320ms in this run because there's no prefetching.

[02:45] Marta: Hmm that P95 is above our 200ms target. Where's the major latency coming from?
[02:51] Priya: Two places: model decoding time for the long-gen requests and scheduling delay because small batches are inefficient. Also KV misses add retreival latency if we do synchronous lookups.
[03:05] Priya: Now Sim 2 - enable prefix/KV cache with a 30% hit rate (conservative estimate based on your repetitive system prompts), and allow small batching window of 10ms to increase batch size to ~3.5. Result: P95 drops to ~180ms and cost per 1M tokens drops ~22%.
[03:28] Sofia: Wait, small batching window 10ms — doesn't that add latency for single-user queries?
[03:33] Priya: Good point — the window is tiny; it only adds a few ms on average. Because your traffic has high concurrency, that window actually increases effective batching without a perceivable latency hit. But if you have very spiky, low-concurrency periods, it's less effective.

[03:50] Liam: Can you break down where the 22% savings come from?
[03:54] Priya: Sure — roughly 12% from better GPU utilization due to batching (amortized kernel overhead), 8% from KV/prefix cache avoiding token decoding on repeated prompts, and the rest from micro-optimizations like response-streaming and dynamic token quantization where applicable.

[04:12] Evan: We also included a fallback policy in the sim — when the cache hit is below 10% we avoid prefetch and instead lean on smaller batch sizing to maintain latency. That keeps the cost/latency balance sane under weird traffic.

[04:26] Marta: On the cache hits — what's realistic for prefix cache? We're worried about diversity of user prompts.
[04:32] Priya: For many assistants, prefix cache hit rates between 20-40% are typical if you cache system prompts, repeated onboarding steps, and common question templates. If your product has more freeform user text, the hit rate will be lower. The console can estimate this using shingled fingerprinting heuristics.

[04:52] [05:00] (audio blip)

[05:05] Priya: Sim 3 - aggressive prefetch/pipeline: we precompute KV cache for the first token of likely next turns and keep a 15 minute session TTL. Batch window 20ms, session affinity enabled. This pushes batch size average to 7.1 and drops token spend by ~34% but increases tail latency on cold sessions if we mispredict. P95 in this sim is 210ms though P90 is under 150ms.
[05:36] Marta: That's interesting — so there's a trade-off that aggressive prefetching gives big cost wins but can hurt worst-case latency?
[05:42] Priya: Exactly. If your SLOs are strict on P95, we recommend a hybrid — prefetch for warm sessions and degrade to smaller batch / reserved capacity for cold paths. Redwood's routing can split traffic by session heat.

[05:58] Liam: Do we need Dedicated capacity to make batching that big, or can hosted do it?
[06:02] Priya: You can achieve this on hosted for most traffic, because we pool requests across customers and micro-batch aggressively. However, Dedicated gives you more predictable tail latency and capacity guarantees. Hosted might occasionally route to fallback variants under extreme load, which slightly changes economics.

[06:19] Sofia: On the security front, Marta wants to confirm: will our cached prefixes include any PII? Our product sometimes uses user names inside system prompts.
[06:28] Evan: Good callout. You can configure redaction hooks before caching. On Private or Dedicated we can integrate KMS and HSM, and the console flags when cache entries contain sensitive tokens. We'll share our security playbook.

[06:42] Priya: Back to sims — Sim 4 is TTL sensitivity: we sweep session TTL from 5m to 45m keeping prefetch heuristics the same. At 5m TTL, cache hit drops to ~14% and cost savings are minimal; at 30m TTL you hit diminishing returns after around 30% hit because the marginal unique prompts increase. So we usually recommend TTL 15-25m for multi-turn assistants.

[07:12] Marta: That aligns with our product — 30m session window. Would moving to 20m risk losing UX?
[07:18] Sofia: Our PM stance — we can tolerate up to 45s extra think time at session boundaries, but not a full context loss. 20m might be okay if we keep immediate context in a short-lived session cache.

[07:32] Priya: Also worth noting — prefix caching is most effective when you can isolate the stable part of the prompt (system + instructions). For freeform user text, KV caching of only deterministic system phrases yields biggest wins.

[07:47] Evan: Quick demo toggle — I'm switching to the console's cost-model panel (link: https://console.redwood.ai/optimize/vep/cost-sim). You can upload your price-per-GPU and your internal cost to compare. Priya, can you run a sensitivity on model size?

[08:05] Priya: Sure — switch to model variants. Baseline uses an open LLM (we'll call it "redwood-2b" in the sim). If you swap to a 4B variant with better decode throughput, you see higher per-token cost but lower latency per token — which can reduce overall spend if it reduces turn count or early-stopping. For Vesper, the sim shows 4B gives slightly better tail latency but cost is 12% higher; with caching it's a net wash.

[08:36] Liam: Could quantization help here? We've experimented with int8 but saw some quality drop.
[08:41] Priya: We support mixed-precision and per-layer quantization profiles. Optimize recommends quantization only for non-sensitive models or for paths where generation quality isn't customer-visible. We also tie quality evals to prompt sets so we don't accidentally regress.

[08:58] Marta: About the fallback policy — can we set different policies for different endpoints? e.g., stricter SLO for payments flow
[09:04] Priya: Yep. Routing and per-route SLOs let you specify canary policies, fallback models, and capacity tiers. Payments flow could be pinned to Dedicated nodes with minimal batching and no prefetch to guarantee P95.

[09:20] [09:30] (Speaker tag confusion) Speaker 3: uh, can you repeat the prefetch heuristics?

[09:36] Priya: Sure. Prefetch heuristics are basically a probabilistic classifier that predicts likely next tokens given recent turns. We score candidates and precompute KV entries for tokens with score above threshold. Threshold tuning balances hit-rate vs wasted compute.

[09:51] Sofia: How often do prefetched entries become stale or wrong? There's a risk of prefetching the wrong branch and burning compute.
[09:58] Priya: True — wasted prefetch is a cost. The console sim models prefetch accuracy and assigns a cost for wasted compute. For your trace we saw a prefetch accuracy around 62% at the aggressive threshold; at conservative threshold accuracy goes up to 78% but hit-rate drops. It's the classic precision/recall tradeoff.

[10:20] Marta: For compliance: we use SSO (SAML) and strict audit trails. Do you log cache evictions and accesses?
[10:28] Evan: Yes, we keep audit logs for cache writes/reads; on Private/Dedicated you can retain logs per your retention policy. We'll put the SOC2 + audit log specifics in the security packet.

[10:38] Priya: I'm going to run a combined sim now — batch window sweep [5ms, 10ms, 25ms, 50ms] x TTL [10, 20, 30m] x prefetch thresholds. This is a 9-point grid. On the left is cost per 1M tokens, on the right is P95.

[10:58] [11:10] (simulation running noise, Priya narrates)
[11:15] Priya: Ok results: best balanced config at your current traffic is 10ms window, 20m TTL, prefetch threshold conservative — yields ~26% cost savings and P95 195ms. The aggressive config pushes savings to 36% but P95 rises to 225ms.

[11:35] Liam: Is there an easy way to validate this live without impacting production? We want to be confident before rolling wide.
[11:41] Priya: Yep — we recommend sandbox pilot with traffic mirroring. You can mirror a percentage of live requests into Redwood's sandbox (no user-facing impact) and we run the exact same policy and measure hit rates/latency. You can also run canary rollout on a small subset of users.

[11:58] Marta: How does session affinity interact with horizontal scaling? If we route to multiple GPUs, will KV cache misses spike?
[12:05] Priya: We use sticky session routing for sessionized caches. In Dedicated you can pin session groups to node pools. For hosted we maintain session affinity within a regional pool and propagate KV cache metadata to the runtime cluster to reduce cross-node misses. There's some replication cost but it's modeled in the sim.

[12:24] Evan: Competitor question — someone asked earlier about doing this on our side, like running the open-source runtime. How do we compare?

[12:31] Priya: If you self-host, you get full control and potentially lower raw infra cost but you pay engineering time and you miss our routing, dynamic fallback, and Optimize tooling. We also maintain kernel optimizations and model compilation which are non-trivial. The sim can import your cloud GPU unit costs to compare TCO.

[12:46] Sofia: For pilot — what telemetry do we need to provide? You mentioned request trace, sequence lengths, and concurrency. Anything else?
[12:53] Priya: Request IDs, timestamps, token counts, per-turn role (system/user/assistant), and indication of any deterministic system text. Also a mapping of endpoints and critical SLOs. That's enough for a high-fidelity sim.

[13:06] Marta: We have one technical deep-dive we want scheduled — Liam wants to go deep on KV eviction policies and the memory footprint on the GPU for cached KV. Can you set that up with an SE deep dive?
[13:16] Evan: Yes — Priya will lead an SE deep dive. We'll propose a date.

[13:21] Priya: Quick note on memory footprint — prefix KV entries are stored in optimized KV structures; we keep hot entries on node RAM and cold entries on remote store. For very large session state we use TTLs and compaction heuristics. Memory pressure is modeled and shown as a projected footprint per 1M active sessions.

[13:40] [13:50] (short pause)

[13:55] Priya: I'm toggling the console to show the runbook suggestions — Optimize suggests: 1) start with TTL 20m, 2) 10ms batch window during business hours, 3) conservative prefetch threshold, 4) enable session affinity for chat endpoints, 5) pilot micro-mirroring for two weeks.

[14:17] Marta: Those are actionable. Can you attach a CSV of the 9 configs you demoed? We want to plug our internal cost model.
[14:24] Priya: Yep will send. That's the action item Priya - export batch-size sims and share CSV.

[14:31] Liam: About metrics: what dashboards will we see in Redwood Console during the pilot?

[14:36] Evan: You get per-route P50/P90/P95, cache hit/miss rates, prefetched wasted compute %, cost per token, and a token-level cost attribution per model. We also expose token-level traces for debugging.

[14:50] Sofia: Any gotchas for streaming responses? We stream partial tokens to user as they generate.

[14:55] Priya: Streaming reduces perceived latency but complicates batching slightly because you may need to flush partial outputs. Optimize accounts for streaming and recommends lower batching window for streaming endpoints or enabling incremental batching.

[15:10] [15:20] (customer question about encryption) Marta: Can cached KV be encrypted with customer-managed keys?
[15:25] Evan: Yes — on Dedicated and Private we integrate with KMS/HSM; cached entries at rest are encrypted and access requires RBAC. We'll include integration notes.

[15:36] Priya: I'm going to show one more micro-sim — cost curve as you scale concurrency 100 -> 1000 rps with chosen balanced config. At low concurrency caching isn't that effective (hit rates drop), but after ~150 rps you start to see the batching gains accumulate. That's why your peak concurrency 420 rps is in the sweet spot.

[15:58] Liam: Good to know. If we lower TTL during off-hours, can we dynamically change these policies by schedule?
[16:03] Priya: Absolutely. We expose time-based policy overrides so you can be aggressive during daytime and conservative at night, or vice versa.

[16:13] Sofia: Regarding cost attribution — can we split by feature? e.g. payments vs support chat
[16:19] Evan: Yes per-route cost attribution can be enabled; you'd tag endpoints and we'll surface costs per tag in the console and a breakdown CSV.

[16:29] [16:40] (brief clarification)

[16:44] Marta: Let's talk pilot sizing. What do you recommend for a two-week pilot? 5% mirrored traffic or run canary on 2% of users?

[16:52] Priya: For a conservative start, 5% mirrored traffic to sandbox gives you accurate hit-rate and performance metrics without user impact. If you want end-to-end validation including routing behavior, a 1-2% canary is good.

[17:04] Liam: Any specific logging or labels we should add to our requests to help correlate?

[17:08] Priya: Include request-id, session-id, endpoint name, and a 'feature_tag' if you want per-feature attribution. Also include sample-quality flags if responses are sensitive.

[17:20] Evan: Security/Legal note — we'll attach a procurement checklist and the standard DPA. If Private deployment needed, that's a separate conversation re: on-prem packaging.

[17:31] Marta: We're likely to try hosted first and then evaluate Dedicated if tails or compliance require it.

[17:36] Sofia: Timeline: we want a pilot in the next 2-3 weeks. Is that achievable?

[17:39] Evan: Yes. We'll need the sample trace and an internal sponsor to approve the mirror. We'll send a pilot runbook after this call.

[17:48] Priya: A couple more lightning Qs — about cache eviction: we use LRU with weightings and hotlist pinning for critical prefixes. You can set eviction budgets per namespace.

[17:59] Liam: How do you reconcile cache privacy with multi-tenant hosted pooling?

[18:05] Priya: Multi-tenant pooling never exposes cache entries cross-tenant. Keys are namespaced and encrypted. But if you need complete isolation we suggest Dedicated.

[18:15] Marta: Suppose we want to optimize purely for cost and accept a small latency increase — is the console able to generate a single-number recommendation? e.g., "save 30%, P95 excepted"

[18:23] Priya: Yes there's a savings optimization slider that biases the recommendations for cost vs latency. It will summarize the tradeoff and provide an actionable config.

[18:33] Sofia: Any inbound support windows for pilot? We might need a 24/7 on-call if we do a canary.
[18:38] Evan: For pilots, standard support covers business hours; extended on-call is available as an add-on. We'll include options in the pricing packet.

[18:48] [18:55] (minor cross-talk)

[19:00] Priya: Wrapping up the technical part — the three configurations we recommend to test in pilot: conservative (10ms, 20m TTL, conservative prefetch), aggressive (25ms, 30m TTL, aggressive prefetch) and fallback-safe (5ms, 15m TTL, no prefetch + reserved capacity for payments endpoints).

[19:20] Marta: That gives us a clear plan. If the pilot shows 25% savings with acceptable latency, we can scope a three-month reserved capacity for Dedicated to lock that in.

[19:30] Evan: Great. I'll send the contract template and pricing tiers. Priya will send the CSV and the sandbox link. We'll also schedule the SE deep dive on KV eviction memory next week.

[19:44] Sofia: One last question, LN: do you expose per-token cost breakout by top tokens? We want to see which prompts are most expensive.
[19:51] Priya: Yes, token-level cost attribution shows hot tokens and hot prefixes. You can use that to rewrite prompts and save cost.

[20:02] [20:10] (closing remarks)

[20:12] Evan: Thanks all, good session. Quick recap in chat and we'll follow up.
[20:17] Marta: Thanks, Evan, Priya. Appreciate the demo.
[20:19] Liam: Thanks.
[20:20] Sofia: Bye.

Notes: The timestamps here approximate, the call ran about 54 minutes; second half included a 30-minute Q/A and deep technical back-and-forth on KV memory details that Priya agreed to cover in follow-up SE deep-dive because it required diagrams and code snippets. Links/Artifacts referenced: Sandbox sim link (console.redwood.ai/optimize/sandbox/vep), Cost sim CSV export (to be attached), Security packet (to be attached), Pilot runbook (to be attached).

End of transcript.
